pairTitles: 太阳也不是最大的恒星
还有比大角星大得多的恒星
把这样大的恒星放到太阳的位置
pairNotes: 木星的直径约是地球的 11 倍。这里比的是直径，不是质量，也不是两者之间的距离。
太阳的直径约是木星的 10 倍。木星仍是刚才那一颗，只是两者一起用了更小的显示比例。
大角星是红巨星，直径约是太阳的 25 倍。它的大小是估计值；恒星大小不同，这不是“最大恒星”排行榜。
心宿二的直径估计约是太阳的 700 倍，大约能横着排下 28 颗大角星。这是大小估计，不是“宇宙最大恒星”的排名。
大犬座 VY 的直径约是心宿二的 2 倍。这里采用 2012 年干涉观测结合大气模型得到的光球半径估计：1420 ± 120 个太阳半径；画面取中心值。不把外围气体和尘埃算成恒星表面，也不把它称作已确定的最大恒星。
史蒂文森 2-18，也写作 St2-18。这个有条件的估计比大犬座 VY 更大；把它假想放在太阳的位置，轮廓会伸到土星轨道附近。恒星竟然可以这么大！

homeTitles: 太阳和行星组成一个系统

观测范围远大于我们的超星系团
homeNotes: 太阳是恒星，地球和其他行星绕着它运行。太阳系的范围包含很长的轨道距离，不能把它当作一颗更大的球。
银河里有许多恒星，太阳只是其中一颗。黄色标记指出太阳系所在的大致区域；这个标记不代表太阳系的真实大小。
保留刚才的银河，再找到仙女座、三角座和周围的小星系。大麦哲伦云、小麦哲伦云等约 50 个矮星系也属于本星系群；图上的小点只抽样示意，并非完整清单。
这是并排对照，不是从本星系群放大就会进入室女座星系团。两者是不同的邻近结构；星系团通常比星系群拥有更多星系。
在拉尼亚凯亚的流向重建中，本星系群位于外围，室女座星系团等群与团也在这一广大区域。这个范围依据星系运动推断，并不是一层坚固边界；整体通常不受自身引力束缚。
单独放大宇宙网的一个示意片段：群与团分布在丝线和结点附近，中间有相对稀疏的空洞。宇宙网是分布形态，不是套在拉尼亚凯亚外面的一层发光绳网。
这幅画面用圆圈表示从我们这里可观测的范围，圆内的丝线、结点和相对稀疏的空洞与连续拉远终点共用一套示意网，并不是把上一幅拉尼亚凯亚图裁成圆形。拉尼亚凯亚约 5.2 亿光年的跨度不到约 930 亿光年观测范围直径的 1%；中心记号因此被放大为定位符。光传播时宇宙也在膨胀；虚线是观测视界，不是宇宙外墙。

pairTitles: The Sun makes Jupiter look small
The Sun is not the largest star
Put an enormous star in the Sun’s place
pairNotes: Jupiter is about 11 Earth diameters across. We compare diameter, not mass or the distance between them.
The Sun is about 10 Jupiter diameters across. This is the same Jupiter, with both objects now drawn at a smaller common scale.
Arcturus is a red giant about 25 Sun diameters across. Its size is estimated; this is not a ranking of the largest stars.
Antares is estimated at about 700 Sun diameters, or roughly 28 Arcturus diameters across. This is an approximate size, not a ranking of the largest stars.

VY Canis Majoris is about twice the diameter of Antares. We use a 2012 photospheric-radius estimate from interferometry and an atmosphere model: 1420 ± 120 solar radii, drawing the central value. Surrounding gas and dust are not counted as the stellar surface; this is not a claim that it is the largest star.
Stephenson 2-18 is also called St2-18. This conditional estimate is larger than VY Canis Majoris; imagined at the Sun’s place, its outline reaches around Saturn’s orbit. A star can be that big!

homeSideNames: Compare Local Group with Virgo Cluster
Look closer at the cosmic web
homeTitles: The Sun and planets form a system
Our Solar System belongs to the galactic disk
The Milky Way belongs to a group
Side by side: Local Group and Virgo Cluster
Local Group and Virgo share a wider region
Close-up: galaxies trace filaments and knots
Our observing range dwarfs our supercluster
homeNotes: The Sun is a star, with Earth and other planets orbiting it. The system spans large orbital distances; it is not a bigger solid ball.
The galaxy contains many stars; our Sun is one of them. The yellow marker indicates our approximate region, not the Solar System’s physical size.

Keep track of the Milky Way, then find Andromeda, Triangulum and smaller neighbors. Around 50 dwarf galaxies, including the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, also belong to the Local Group. The small points are a sample, not a census.

This is a side-by-side comparison: zooming out from the Local Group does not take us inside the Virgo Cluster. They are different nearby structures; clusters generally contain more galaxies than groups.

In the Laniakea flow reconstruction, the Local Group lies near the edge, while the Virgo Cluster and other groups and clusters share the wider region. Its extent is inferred from galaxy motions, not a hard shell; the region is generally not bound as a whole.

Look closely at one illustrative patch of the cosmic web: groups and clusters gather near filaments and knots, with comparatively sparse voids between. The web describes a distribution, not a glowing layer surrounding Laniakea.

This circle marks the region observable from here. Its filaments, knots and comparatively sparse voids use the same illustrative web as the end of the continuous zoom, rather than cropping the previous Laniakea drawing. Laniakea's roughly 520-million-light-year span is under 1% of the roughly 93-billion-light-year observable diameter, so its center marker is enlarged to stay visible. Space expanded as light traveled; the dashed horizon is an observing limit, not an outer wall.
homeBoundary: Membership illustration · Orbits, planet locations and body sizes are not to scale; the Solar System is not a solid ball.
The external Milky Way view reconstructs structure; it is not a complete photograph taken from outside. Markers, arms and disk are not measurements.
Membership illustration · Three large galaxies and a few dwarf markers are not a complete census. Shapes, directions, sizes and spacing are not to scale.
Side-by-side illustration · The panels do not share a scale. Point counts are not censuses and positions cannot be measured. Pale blue hot gas illustrates X-ray structure, not visible color.
Large-scale structure diagram · The dashed flow region is inferred from a model, not a precise boundary; lines are not physical ropes, and positions cannot be measured here.
Local texture diagram · Filaments, knots and voids do not map real sky positions; bright points are not actual galaxy counts or a ruler for Laniakea's size.

Observable-region diagram · The circle suggests an approximate present-day distance scale. Its fine web, knots and density are statistical illustration, not an all-sky survey or real counts. The central marker is not Laniakea's diameter, and the dashed horizon is no physical edge.

estimateNotes: St2-18 uses about 2150 solar radii derived from log(L/L☉)=5.64 and 3200 K in Fok et al. (2012). Its distance and cluster membership are uncertain and later work questions the association. This is a conditional size estimate, not a precise measurement or a confirmed record.
